old: Its ancestor simply meant something falling into place — by accident, not design.
The root word meant 'a chance event,' before it took on a darker sense of loss.
It's a cousin of 'case,' both falling from the Latin cāsus.
clues: This somber noun for a kind of loss once meant any chance occurrence at all, whether lucky or unlucky.
It names a person killed or injured in a war, disaster or accident, so it is broader than a fatality, since the wounded count too. Its root is a Latin verb meaning 'to fall.'
The saying goes that truth is the first one of war, and in Britain the hospital emergency room is named for it. It shares its Latin root with 'case.'
